claim: ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channels are composed of a pore-forming Kir6.2 potassium channel and a regulatory ABC transporter sulfonylurea receptor 1 (SUR1).
source: ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channels composed of a pore-forming Kir6.2 potassium channel and a regulatory ABC transporter sulfonylurea receptor 1 (SUR1) regulate insulin secretion in pancreatic β-cells to maintain glucose homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: KATP channels regulate insulin secretion in pancreatic β-cells to maintain glucose homeostasis.
source: ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channels composed of a pore-forming Kir6.2 potassium channel and a regulatory ABC transporter sulfonylurea receptor 1 (SUR1) regulate insulin secretion in pancreatic β-cells to maintain glucose homeostasis.
evidence: This is a well-established physiological role of KATP channels supported by extensive literature.

claim: Mutations that impair channel folding or assembly prevent cell surface expression and cause congenital hyperinsulinism.
source: Mutations that impair channel folding or assembly prevent cell surface expression and cause congenital hyperinsulinism.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Structurally diverse KATP inhibitors act as pharmacochaperones to correct mutant channel expression.
source: Structurally diverse KATP inhibitors are known to act as pharmacochaperones to correct mutant channel expression, but the mechanism is unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior work cited in the introduction.

claim: All three drugs (glibenclamide, repaglinide, and carbamazepine) bind within a common pocket in SUR1.
source: We found all three drugs bind within a common pocket in SUR1.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by cryo-EM structural data.

claim: The N-terminus of Kir6.2 is inserted within the central cavity of the SUR1 ABC core, adjacent to the drug binding pocket.
source: Further, we found the N-terminus of Kir6.2 inserted within the central cavity of the SUR1 ABC core, adjacent the drug binding pocket.
evidence: This is a primary structural finding supported by cryo-EM density maps.

claim: Diverse compounds stabilize the Kir6.2 N-terminus within SUR1's ABC core, allowing it to act as a 'handle' for the assembly of metastable mutant SUR1-Kir6.2 complexes.
source: The findings reveal a common mechanism by which diverse compounds stabilize the Kir6.2 N-terminus within SUR1's ABC core, allowing it to act as a firm 'handle' for the assembly of metastable mutant SUR1-Kir6.2 complexes.
evidence: This is the main mechanistic conclusion of the study, supported by structural and functional data.

claim: Four SUR.x subunits form a complex with four subunits of an inwardly rectifying potassium channel, Kir6.1 or Kir6.2.
source: Uniquely, the sulfonylurea receptors SUR1 and SUR2 lack transport activity per se but instead are devoted to forming the ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channels, wherein four SUR.x subunits form a complex with four subunits of an inwardly rectifying potassium channel, Kir6.1 or Kir6.2 (Aittoniemi et al., 2009; Ashcroft and Ashcroft, 1990; Bryan et al., 2007; Nichols, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about KATP channel stoichiometry, supported by multiple citations.

claim: KATP channels are gated by intracellular ATP and ADP.
source: KATP channels are gated by intracellular ATP and ADP, key features which enable them to regulate membrane excitability according to the energetic state of the cell (Nichols, 2006).
evidence: This is a well-established functional property of KATP channels.

claim: Gain-of-function mutations in the SUR1 gene ABCC8 or the Kir6.2 gene KCNJ11 are a major cause of neonatal diabetes.
source: Gain-of-function mutations in the SUR1 gene ABCC8 or the Kir6.2 gene KCNJ11 are a major cause of neonatal diabetes, while loss-of-function mutations result in congenital hyperinsulinism (Ashcroft et al., 2017; Koster et al., 2005; Stanley, 2016).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in ABCC8 or KCNJ11 result in congenital hyperinsulinism.
source: Gain-of-function mutations in the SUR1 gene ABCC8 or the Kir6.2 gene KCNJ11 are a major cause of neonatal diabetes, while loss-of-function mutations result in congenital hyperinsulinism (Ashcroft et al., 2017; Koster et al., 2005; Stanley, 2016).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Severe hyperinsulinism requiring pancreatectomy is often the result of KATP channel mutations that reduce KATP channel density on the β-cell surface by impairing channel biogenesis, assembly, and trafficking.
source: Among the latter, severe hyperinsulinism requiring pancreatectomy to prevent life-threatening hypoglycemia is often the result of KATP channel mutations that reduce KATP channel density on the β-cell surface by impairing channel biogenesis, assembly, and trafficking (referred to as trafficking mutations hereinafter) (Huopio et al., 2002; Vajravelu and De León, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: KATP channel inhibitors commonly used to treat Type 2 diabetes are efficient pharmacochaperones for correcting surface expression defects of certain trafficking-impaired mutant KATP channels.
source: Previously, we showed that KATP channel inhibitors commonly used to treat Type 2 diabetes are efficient pharmacochaperones for correcting surface expression defects of certain trafficking-impaired mutant KATP channels, including sulfonylureas (SUs) and glinides (Yan et al., 2004; Yan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on prior work by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: Most trafficking mutations identified to date are in SUR1, perhaps due to its large size compared to Kir6.2.
source: Most trafficking mutations identified to date are in SUR1, perhaps due to its large size compared to Kir6.2 (Martin et al., 2013; Snider et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an observation from prior studies with a speculative explanation.

claim: The SUR1 protein has an N-terminal transmembrane domain referred to as TMD0 that interacts directly with the Kir6.2 subunit.
source: The SUR1 protein has an N-terminal transmembrane domain referred to as TMD0 that interacts directly with the Kir6.2 subunit (Babenko and Bryan, 2003; Chan et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2017; Li et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2017b; Schwappach et al., 2000), followed by a cytoplasmic loop termed L0, and then the ABC core structure comprising two transmembrane domains TMD1 and TMD2 and two nucleotide binding domains NBD1 and NBD2 (Aguilar-Bryan et al., 1995; Martin et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: SUs and glinides have to date only corrected defects caused by mutations located in TMD0.
source: Of particular interest, while trafficking mutations are found throughout SUR1, SUs and glinides have to date only corrected defects caused by mutations located in TMD0, the domain contacting Kir6.2.
evidence: This is an observation from prior functional studies.

claim: Carbamazepine (CBZ) corrects KATP channel trafficking defects and is effective only for mutations in TMD0 of SUR1.
source: Recently, we found that carbamazepine (CBZ), an anticonvulsant structurally not related to SUs and glinides, also corrects KATP channel trafficking defects (Chen et al., 2013; Sampson et al., 2013) and surprisingly is effective only for mutations in TMD0 of SUR1 (Devaraneni et al., 2015; Martin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on prior work by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: CBZ inhibits KATP channel activity by reducing channel Po and abolishing channel responsiveness to MgADP.
source: Furthermore, like SUs and glinides, CBZ inhibits KATP channel activity by reducing channel Po and abolishing channel responsiveness to MgADP (Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies, supported by citation.

claim: A FLAG-tagged hamster SUR1 and a rat Kir6.2 (95% and 96% identical to human, respectively) were overexpressed in the insulinoma cell line INS-1 for structure determination.
source: For structure determination, a FLAG-tagged hamster SUR1 and a rat Kir6.2 (95% and 96% identical to human, respectively) were overexpressed in the insulinoma cell line INS-1, and the channel complex affinity purified via the FLAG-epitope tag as described for our recent cryoEM structure determination of KATP bound to GBC and ATP (Martin et al., 2017a; Martin et al., 2017b).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Initial data processing in RELION with C4 symmetry imposed yielded one dominant 3D class for each dataset, with an overall reported resolution ranging from ~4 Å for the RPG/ATP and CBZ/ATP states to ~7 Å for the ATP-only and the apo states.
source: Initial data processing in RELION with C4 symmetry imposed yielded one dominant 3D class for each dataset, with an overall reported resolution ranging from ~4 Å for the RPG/ATP and CBZ/ATP states to ~7 Å for the ATP-only and the apo states (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplements 1–4; Table 1).
evidence: This describes the results of cryo-EM data processing, supported by figures and table.

claim: Focused refinement using symmetry expansion and signal subtraction yielded maps with improved reported resolutions for SUR1: 3.74 Å for the GBC/ATP state, 3.65 Å for the RPG/ATP state, 4.34 Å for the CBZ/ATP state, 4.50 Å for the ATP-only state, and 4.55 Å for the apo state.
source: This yielded maps with improved reported resolutions for SUR1 as follows: 3.74 Å for the GBC/ATP state, 3.65 Å for the RPG/ATP state, 4.34 Å for the CBZ/ATP state, 4.50 Å for the ATP-only state, and 4.55 Å for the apo state using the FSC cutoff of 0.143 (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the results of focused refinement, supported by Table 1.

claim: In all structures determined in the presence of pharmacochaperones and ATP, the Kir6.2 tetramer is in a closed conformation.
source: In all structures determined in the presence of pharmacochaperones and ATP, the Kir6.2 tetramer is in a closed conformation (Figure 1C), and the SUR1's ABC core in an 'inward-facing' conformation wherein the NBD1 and NBD2 are separated (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The SUR1's ABC core is in an 'inward-facing' conformation wherein the NBD1 and NBD2 are separated in all structures determined in the presence of pharmacochaperones and ATP.
source: In all structures determined in the presence of pharmacochaperones and ATP, the Kir6.2 tetramer is in a closed conformation (Figure 1C), and the SUR1's ABC core in an 'inward-facing' conformation wherein the NBD1 and NBD2 are separated (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The dominant class emerging from 3D classification for the ATP-only state as well as the apo state presented a similar conformation, with Kir6.2 tetramer closed and SUR1 inward-facing.
source: Interestingly, the dominant class emerging from 3D classification for the ATP-only state as well as the apo state presented a similar conformation, with Kir6.2 tetramer closed and SUR1 inward-facing (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data, shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: A dominant inward-facing conformation in the absence of ligand was also observed in another ABC transporter, the multidrug resistance protein MRP1.
source: Of note, a dominant inward-facing conformation in the absence of ligand was also observed in another ABC transporter, the multidrug resistance protein MRP1 (Johnson and Chen, 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison to another ABC transporter, supported by citation.

claim: The closed channel conformation is the most stable for the apo state under the experimental conditions (no ATP and no exogenous PIP2).
source: These observations suggest the closed channel conformation is the most stable for the apo state under our experimental conditions (i.e. no ATP and no exogenous PIP2, a lipid required for KATP channel opening [Nichols, 2006]).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data, with reference to PIP2 requirement.

claim: GBC is lodged in the TM bundle above NBD1.
source: We previously solved the KATP structure in the presence of GBC and ATP, revealing that GBC is lodged in the TM bundle above NBD1 (Martin et al., 2017a), a finding which has been independently confirmed (Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on prior structural work by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: In both the RPG/ATP and CBZ/ATP structures, strong and distinctly shaped cryo-EM densities are observed within the same GBC binding pocket.
source: Here, in both the RPG/ATP and CBZ/ATP structures, we observe strong and distinctly shaped cryo-EM densities within the same GBC binding pocket (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data, shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: The ligand density is absent in the ATP-only and the apo structures.
source: Such density is absent in the ATP-only and the apo structures (Figure 2E and F), supporting assignment as the pharmacochaperone ligand.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data, shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Density for RPG appears compact and palm-shaped, and suggests that the molecule adopts a considerably folded shape upon binding to SUR1.
source: Density for RPG appears compact and palm-shaped, and suggests that the molecule adopts a considerably folded shape upon binding to SUR1 (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data, shown in Figure 2B and supplement.

claim: RPG possesses a carboxyl group adjacent a benzyl group, analogous to the sulfonyl group in GBC that is also adjacent a benzyl group.
source: Interestingly, RPG possesses a carboxyl group adjacent a benzyl group, analogous to the sulfonyl group in GBC that is also adjacent a benzyl group (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a chemical comparison shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Refinement of an RPG molecule into the observed binding pocket density orients the carboxylate towards N1245, R1246, and R1300.
source: Refinement of an RPG molecule into the observed binding pocket density orients this carboxylate towards N1245, R1246, and R1300 (Figure 3A), which coordinate the sulfonyl group in the GBC-bound structure (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from modeling, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Unlike GBC, the RPG density is distant from S1238.
source: However, unlike GBC, the RPG density is distant from S1238.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: An SUR1 S1238Y mutation does not affect RPG's ability to modulate channel function.
source: This explains previous functional data that an SUR1 S1238Y mutation does not affect RPG's ability to modulate channel function (Hansen et al., 2002; Yan et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies, supported by citations.

claim: There are subtle rearrangements within the binding pocket between GBC- and RPG-bound states.
source: Interestingly, although similar in overall structures, we noted subtle rearrangements within the binding pocket between GBC- and RPG-bound states (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from comparing the two structures, shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: W1297 in RPG is flipped down towards the ligand compared to the GBC-bound state.
source: The most obvious is in W1297, which in RPG is flipped down towards the ligand.
evidence: This is a structural observation from comparing the two structures.

claim: There is sufficient flexibility of the binding pocket to accommodate diverse compounds with high affinity.
source: Thus, there is sufficient flexibility of the binding pocket to accommodate diverse compounds with high affinity.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural observations of different ligands binding.

claim: CBZ is a smaller molecule with molecular weight about half of that of GBC and RPG.
source: CBZ is a smaller molecule with molecular weight about half of that of GBC and RPG (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a chemical fact shown in Figure 2G.

claim: In the CBZ-bound SUR1 structure the cryoEM density corresponding to the ligand has a size and shape that markedly resembles GBC.
source: However, in the CBZ-bound SUR1 structure the cryoEM density corresponding to the ligand has a size and shape that markedly resembles GBC (Figure 2C and D), with one end pointing towards S1238.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data, shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The close proximity to S1238 is in agreement with the finding that mutation of S1238 to Y diminishes the ability of CBZ to both inhibit and chaperone the channel.
source: While the close proximity to S1238 is in agreement with our previous finding that mutation of S1238 to Y diminishes the ability of CBZ to both inhibit and chaperone the channel (Devaraneni et al., 2015), the density is too large to be fitted by a single CBZ molecule (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a comparison of structural data with prior functional data, supported by citation.

claim: The CBZ density is too large to be fitted by a single CBZ molecule.
source: While the close proximity to S1238 is in agreement with our previous finding that mutation of S1238 to Y diminishes the ability of CBZ to both inhibit and chaperone the channel (Devaraneni et al., 2015), the density is too large to be fitted by a single CBZ molecule (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data, shown in Figure 2C and supplement.

claim: CBZ may bind as a dimer to occupy the entire binding pocket.
source: Thus, an intriguing possibility is that CBZ may bind as a dimer to occupy the entire binding pocket (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the structural data, shown in Figure 2 supplement 1C.

claim: This is the first protein structure determined in complex with CBZ.
source: To our knowledge this is the first protein structure determined in complex with CBZ.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the structural finding.

claim: Alanine mutation of five select SUR1 residues lining the binding pocket reduced the chaperone ability of the drugs to a variable extent for each of the binding site mutations tested in the F27S background.
source: This chaperone ability of the drugs was reduced to a variable extent for each of the binding site mutations tested in the F27S background (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a functional result from Western blot experiments, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: While the sensitivity profile is very similar for GBC and CBZ, that for RPG is slightly different, in particular to the R1246A mutation.
source: Interestingly, we noted that while the sensitivity profile is very similar for GBC and CBZ, that for RPG is slightly different, in particular to the R1246A mutation.
evidence: This is an observation from the functional data in Figure 3C.

claim: Despite sharing a common binding pocket, RPG forms distinct chemical interactions with surrounding residues compared to GBC and CBZ.
source: This suggests despite sharing a common binding pocket, RPG forms distinct chemical interactions with surrounding residues compared to GBC and CBZ.
evidence: This is an inference from the functional data showing different sensitivity profiles.

claim: CBZ, RPG, and GBC exert their pharmacochaperoning effects by binding to a common binding pocket.
source: The combined structural and functional data presented above provide strong evidence that CBZ, RPG, and GBC exert their pharmacochaperoning effects by binding to a common binding pocket we have here identified.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the combined structural and functional data.

claim: The N-terminal ~30 amino acids of Kir6.2 (KNt) is critical for channel assembly, gating, and interaction with sulfonylureas and glinides.
source: The N-terminal ~30 amino acids of Kir6.2 (referred to as KNt hereinafter) has been known to be critical for channel assembly, gating, and interaction with sulfonylureas and glinides.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: Deletion of KNt significantly increases channel open probability.
source: Early studies showed that deletion of KNt significantly increases channel open probability (Babenko et al., 1999; Koster et al., 1999b; Reimann et al., 1999; Shyng et al., 1997), reduces ATP inhibition, and renders the channel less sensitive to sulfonylureas (Koster et al., 1999a; Reimann et al., 1999).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies, supported by citations.

claim: Deletion of KNt reduces ATP inhibition and renders the channel less sensitive to sulfonylureas.
source: Early studies showed that deletion of KNt significantly increases channel open probability (Babenko et al., 1999; Koster et al., 1999b; Reimann et al., 1999; Shyng et al., 1997), reduces ATP inhibition, and renders the channel less sensitive to sulfonylureas (Koster et al., 1999a; Reimann et al., 1999).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies, supported by citations.

claim: KNt appears to contribute to GBC binding.
source: KNt also appears to contribute to GBC binding (Kühner et al., 2012; Vila-Carriles et al., 2007), and is necessary for high affinity interaction with RPG (Hansen et al., 2005; Kühner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies, supported by citations.

claim: KNt is necessary for high affinity interaction with RPG.
source: KNt also appears to contribute to GBC binding (Kühner et al., 2012; Vila-Carriles et al., 2007), and is necessary for high affinity interaction with RPG (Hansen et al., 2005; Kühner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies, supported by citations.

claim: Deletion of amino acids 2–5 from the KNt shifts the binding affinity of RPG by more than 30-fold.
source: Deletion of amino acids 2–5 from the KNt shifts the binding affinity of RPG by more than 30-fold (Kühner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies, supported by citation.

claim: KNt is critical for channel assembly and pharmacochaperoning.
source: Moreover, KNt is critical for channel assembly and pharmacochaperoning (Devaraneni et al., 2015; Schwappach et al., 2000).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies, supported by citations.

claim: Removal of KNt markedly reduces the ability of GBC and CBZ to rescue SUR1-TMD0 trafficking mutations.
source: Removal of KNt markedly reduces the ability of GBC and CBZ to rescue SUR1-TMD0 trafficking mutations (Devaraneni et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies, supported by citation.

claim: p-azidophenylalanine genetically incorporated at Kir6.2 amino acid position 12 or 18 was photocrosslinked to SUR1 and the extent of crosslinking increased in the presence of GBC or CBZ.
source: Our recent studies showing that p-azidophenylalanine genetically incorporated at Kir6.2 amino acid position 12 or 18 was photocrosslinked to SUR1 and that the extent of crosslinking increased in the presence of GBC or CBZ further suggest physical interactions between KNt and SUR1 in a drug-sensitive manner (Devaraneni et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on prior crosslinking studies by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: KNt is located near the pharmacochaperone binding pocket.
source: Taken together, these studies led us to hypothesize that KNt is located near the pharmacochaperone binding pocket we have identified.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on prior functional and crosslinking data.

claim: The three pharmacochaperone-bound SUR1 structures revealed significant and continuous cryo-EM density immediately adjacent to the drug binding site, especially in the RPG-bound map.
source: Close examination of the three pharmacochaperone-bound SUR1 structures reconstructed using focused refinement indeed revealed significant and continuous cryo-EM density immediately adjacent to the drug binding site, especially in the RPG-bound map (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data, shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: This density appears as a roughly linear peptide inserting between the two TMDs of SUR1 from the intracellular side.
source: This density appears as a roughly linear peptide inserting between the two TMDs of SUR1 from the intracellular side.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: By filtering the GBC/ATP and RPG/ATP maps to a lower resolution (6 Å), contiguous density was observed that extends out of the SUR1's central cavity and connects to the density of the first structured residue R32 in Kir6.2.
source: By filtering the GBC/ATP and RPG/ATP maps to a lower resolution (6 Å), we were able to see contiguous density that extends out of the SUR1's central cavity and connects to the density of the first structured residue R32 in Kir6.2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data, shown in Figure 4 supplement 1.

claim: Wu et al. pointed out a density in the SUR1's central cavity that is nearly contiguous with the Kir6.2 cytoplasmic domain in the published GBC-bound structure and proposed it to be the N-terminus of Kir6.2.
source: Of note, a recent report by Wu et al. also pointed out a density in the SUR1's central cavity that is nearly contiguous with the Kir6.2 cytoplasmic domain in our published GBC-bound structure and proposed it to be the N-terminus of Kir6.2 (Wu et al., 2018) (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a reference to another study that made a similar observation, supported by citation.

claim: The KNt density is also seen in the ATP-only reconstruction though not as strong or well-defined as in the drug-bound reconstructions.
source: Of note, the KNt density is also seen in the ATP-only reconstruction though not as strong or well-defined as in the drug-bound reconstructions (i.e., the density disappears at lower σ values for the ATP-only map), but is largely absent in the apo state structure (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The KNt density is largely absent in the apo state structure.
source: Of note, the KNt density is also seen in the ATP-only reconstruction though not as strong or well-defined as in the drug-bound reconstructions (i.e., the density disappears at lower σ values for the ATP-only map), but is largely absent in the apo state structure (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM data, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: KNt enters into the central cavity of the inward-facing SUR1 even in the absence of drugs, and drug binding stabilizes the location of KNt in the central cavity.
source: This indicates KNt enters into the central cavity of the inward-facing SUR1 even in the absence of drugs, and that drug binding stabilizes the location of KNt in the central cavity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural observations comparing drug-bound and drug-free states.

claim: Deletion of amino acids 2–5 or 2–10 increasingly reduced the ability of the pharmacochaperones to correct the processing defect of the F27S TMD0 mutant SUR1.
source: We found that deletion of amino acids 2–5 or 2–10 increasingly reduced the ability of the pharmacochaperones to correct the processing defect of the F27S TMD0 mutant SUR1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a functional result from Western blot experiments, shown in Figure 4 supplement 2B.

claim: The same Kir6.2 N-terminal deletion mutations also reduced the maturation of WT SUR1 and the ability of pharmacochaperones to enhance WT SUR1 maturation.
source: Interestingly, the same Kir6.2 N-terminal deletion mutations also reduced the maturation of WT SUR1 and the ability of pharmacochaperones to enhance WT SUR1 maturation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a functional result from Western blot experiments, shown in Figure 4 supplement 2C.

claim: KNt binds to the central cavity of the SUR1 ABC core and stabilizes SUR1-Kir6.2 association by simultaneous interaction with multiple SUR1 TMD helices to facilitate complex assembly.
source: These structural and functional observations lead us to propose that KNt binds to the central cavity of the SUR1 ABC core and stabilizes SUR1-Kir6.2 association by simultaneous interaction with multiple SUR1 TMD helices to facilitate complex assembly.
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on the structural and functional data.

claim: This mechanism is important for efficient biogenesis of WT channels and likely underlies the ability of pharmacochaperones to enhance WT channel biogenesis efficiency and rescue mutant channel assembly.
source: This mechanism not only is important for efficient biogenesis of WT channels but also likely underlies the ability of pharmacochaperones to enhance WT channel biogenesis efficiency and rescue mutant channel assembly (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference about the broader implications of the mechanism.

claim: One of the inter-SUR1-Kir6.2 crosslinks identified connected Kir6.2 lysine five and SUR1 lysine 602.
source: One of the inter-SUR1-Kir6.2 crosslinks we identified connected Kir6.2 lysine five and SUR1 lysine 602 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), which is near the drug binding site in our structural model.
evidence: This is a result from crosslinking/mass spectrometry experiments, shown in Figure 4 supplement 3.

claim: SUR1 lysine 602 is near the drug binding site in the structural model.
source: One of the inter-SUR1-Kir6.2 crosslinks we identified connected Kir6.2 lysine five and SUR1 lysine 602 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), which is near the drug binding site in our structural model.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the model.

claim: The distance between α carbons (Cα) of the crosslinked lysines in the model is ~18 Å, which is within the reported range for the linker.
source: The distance between α carbons (Cα) of the crosslinked lysines in our model is ~18 Å, which is within the reported range for the linker (Brodie et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a measurement from the structural model, compared to known linker length.

claim: This result provides the first evidence for the physical proximity of KNt to the SUR1 ABC core central cavity.
source: This result provides the first evidence for the physical proximity of KNt to the SUR1 ABC core central cavity.
evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the crosslinking result.

claim: Crosslinking of KNt with SUR1-C1142 would trap KNt within the SUR1 ABC core and reduce channel open probability.
source: We hypothesized that crosslinking of KNt with SUR1-C1142 would trap KNt within the SUR1 ABC core and reduce channel open probability, based on previous studies that deletion of KNt increases channel open probability (Babenko and Bryan, 2002; Babenko et al., 1999; Koster et al., 1999a; Reimann et al., 1999; Shyng et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on prior functional studies, supported by citations.

claim: Co-expression of Kir6.2-L2C with WT SUR1 resulted in channels that displayed current recovery upon exposure to DTT following the initial exposure to I2.
source: Strikingly, co-expression of Kir6.2-L2C with WT SUR1 resulted in channels that displayed current recovery upon exposure to DTT (10 mM) following the initial exposure to I2 (250 µM).
evidence: This is a functional result from electrophysiology experiments.

claim: None of the other Kir6.2 cysteine mutations showed DTT-induced current recovery when co-expressed with SUR1-C1142.
source: Importantly, none of the other Kir6.2 cysteine mutations showed DTT-induced current recovery when co-expressed with SUR1-C1142 (R4C shown as an example in Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a functional result from electrophysiology experiments, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: WT channels or channels formed by co-expressing Kir6.2-L2C and SUR1-C1142A failed to show current reversal in DTT.
source: WT channels or channels formed by co-expressing Kir6.2-L2C and a SUR1 in which C1142 was mutated to an alanine (C1142A) also failed to show current reversal in DTT.
evidence: This is a functional result from electrophysiology experiments.

claim: More than half of the WT-SUR1/Kir6.2-L2C patches (8 out of 14) showed significant DTT-induced current recovery while none of the other channels tested did (>40 patches).
source: Regardless, our observations that more than half of the WT-SUR1/Kir6.2-L2C patches (8 out of 14) showed significant DTT-induced current recovery while none of the other channels tested did (>40 patches) support crosslinking between SUR1-C1142 and Kir6.2-L2C.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the electrophysiology results.

claim: The structural and functional data is consistent with the idea that insertion of KNt into the central cavity of SUR1 ABC core serves as a mechanism to reduce channel open probability, in addition to promoting channel assembly.
source: Together our structural and functional data is consistent with the idea that insertion of KNt into the central cavity of SUR1 ABC core serves as a mechanism to reduce channel open probability, in addition to promoting channel assembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the combined structural and functional data.

claim: Loss of membrane protein expression due to impaired folding and trafficking underlies numerous human diseases.
source: Loss of membrane protein expression due to impaired folding and trafficking underlies numerous human diseases.
evidence: This is general knowledge about protein folding diseases.

claim: In some cases, such defects can be overcome by small molecule ligands that bind to mutant proteins, referred to as pharmacochaperones.
source: In some cases, such defects can be overcome by small molecule ligands that bind to mutant proteins, referred to as pharmacochaperones (Bernier et al., 2004; Hanrahan et al., 2013; Powers et al., 2009; Ringe and Petsko, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about pharmacochaperones, supported by citations.

claim: Detailed structural mechanisms of how pharmacochaperones work are in most cases not well understood.
source: Although significant progress has been made in discovering pharmacochaperones, as exemplified for the CFTR mutation ΔF508 (Mijnders et al., 2017; Pedemonte et al., 2005; Veit et al., 2018), detailed structural mechanisms of how these compounds work are in most cases not well understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Occupancy of the pharmacochaperone binding site stabilizes the insertion of KNt into the central cavity of the SUR1 ABC core.
source: Rather, occupancy of the pharmacochaperone binding site stabilizes the insertion of KNt into the central cavity of the SUR1 ABC core, an otherwise labile interaction that is nonetheless crucial for assembly and trafficking of the channel complex out of the ER (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion from the study, illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: The KNt-SUR1 interaction is labile but crucial for assembly and trafficking of the channel complex out of the ER.
source: Rather, occupancy of the pharmacochaperone binding site stabilizes the insertion of KNt into the central cavity of the SUR1 ABC core, an otherwise labile interaction that is nonetheless crucial for assembly and trafficking of the channel complex out of the ER (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion from the study, illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: GBC, RPG, and CBZ fail to chaperone TMD0 trafficking mutants in the SUR1RKR-AAA background.
source: Supporting this notion, GBC, RPG, and CBZ fail to chaperone TMD0 trafficking mutants in the SUR1RKR-AAA background, a variant in which the RKR ER retention signal has been mutated to AAA to allow Kir6.2-independent trafficking to the cell surface (Devaraneni et al., 2015; Yan et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies, supported by citations.

claim: Progressive deletion of KNt (2-5, 2-10) renders pharmacochaperones less and less effective in rescuing the trafficking mutant.
source: Progressive deletion of KNt (2-5, 2-10) renders pharmacochaperones less and less effective in rescuing the trafficking mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), likely due to progressive weakening of pharmacochaperone-dependent KNt-SUR1 interactions.
evidence: This is a functional result with an interpretation, shown in Figure 4 supplement 2B.

claim: Progressive deletion of KNt (2-5, 2-10) markedly reduces the biogenesis efficiency of WT channels and makes pharmacochaperones less and less effective in enhancing the biogenesis efficiency of the channel.
source: Importantly, progressive deletion of KNt (2-5, 2-10) also markedly reduces the biogenesis efficiency of WT channels and makes pharmacochaperones less and less effective in enhancing the biogenesis efficiency of the channel (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a functional result shown in Figure 4 supplement 2C.

claim: Insertion of KNt into the central cavity of the SUR1-ABC core is a principal mechanism to stabilize SUR1-Kir6.2 interaction during channel assembly.
source: These results lead us to propose insertion of KNt into the central cavity of the SUR1-ABC core as a principal mechanism to stabilize SUR1-Kir6.2 interaction during channel assembly.
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on the functional data.

claim: During normal channel assembly, insertion of KNt into the SUR1 central cavity facilitates interactions between SUR1-TMD0 and Kir6.2.
source: We suggest that during normal channel assembly, insertion of KNt into the SUR1 central cavity facilitates interactions between SUR1-TMD0 and Kir6.2.
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on the data.

claim: Once assembled, the interactions between SUR1-TMD0 and Kir6.2 become the primary anchor holding the two subunits together and the KNt-SUR1 interaction adopts the role of gating regulation.
source: Once assembled, the interactions between SUR1-TMD0 and Kir6.2 become the primary anchor holding the two subunits together and the KNt-SUR1 interaction, rather than serving a structural role, adopts the role of gating regulation (see below).
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal about the dual role of KNt.

claim: By occupying the central cavity of the SUR1 ABC core, KNt prevents NBD dimerization and stabilizes SUR1 in an inward-facing conformation, thereby abolishing the ability of Mg-nucleotides to stimulate channel activity.
source: First, by occupying the central cavity of the SUR1 ABC core, KNt prevents NBD dimerization and stabilizes SUR1 in an inward-facing conformation, thereby abolishing the ability of Mg-nucleotides to stimulate channel activity (Sikimic et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on the structural data, with citation.

claim: By trapping KNt in the central cavity, SUR1 prevents the Kir6.2 tetramer from undergoing conformational changes needed for channel opening.
source: Second, by trapping KNt in the central cavity, SUR1 prevents the Kir6.2 tetramer from undergoing conformational changes needed for channel opening.
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on the structural and functional data.

claim: DTT exposure recovers currents of channels formed by SUR1-C1142 and Kir6.2-L2C previously exposed to I2, indicating crosslinking-induced decrease of channel activity.
source: Our results that DTT exposure recovers currents of channels formed by SUR1-C1142 and Kir6.2-L2C previously exposed to I2 indicates crosslinking-induced decrease of channel activity and lends support to the second mechanism.
evidence: This is a functional result that supports the mechanistic proposal.

claim: Deletion of KNt increased channel open probability and decreased the ability of sulfonylureas to inhibit the channel.
source: It also explains early studies showing that deletion of KNt increased channel open probability and decreased the ability of sulfonylureas to inhibit the channel (Babenko and Bryan, 2002; Koster et al., 1999a; Reimann et al., 1999; Shyng et al., 1997).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies, supported by citations.

claim: Inserting increasing number of amino acids in the linker between SUR1 and Kir6.2 in the SUR1-Kir6.2 fusion channels caused a gradual decrease in channel inhibition by GBC.
source: Interestingly, Wu et al. recently showed that inserting increasing number of amino acids in the linker between SUR1 and Kir6.2 in the SUR1-Kir6.2 fusion channels caused a gradual decrease in channel inhibition by GBC (Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on another study, supported by citation.

claim: KNt acts as a chain which prevents Kir6.2 cytoplasmic domain from rotating to open the channel when trapped in the SUR1's central cavity; increasing the linker length in the fusion protein reduces the tension exerted by the KNt-SUR1 interaction to reduce channel inhibition by GBC.
source: They postulate that KNt acts as a chain which prevents Kir6.2 cytoplasmic domain from rotating to open the channel when trapped in the SUR1's central cavity; increasing the linker length in the fusion protein reduces the tension exerted by the KNt-SUR1 interaction to reduce channel inhibition by GBC.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation from another study.

claim: The KNt density, albeit weaker, is found in the ATP-only structure, suggesting KNt spends significant time in SUR1's ABC core cavity when Kir6.2 is in the ATP-bound closed state.
source: It is worth noting that the KNt density, albeit weaker, is found in the ATP-only structure. This suggests KNt spends significant time in SUR1's ABC core cavity when Kir6.2 is in the ATP-bound closed state.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural observation.

claim: When no ATP is bound to Kir6.2, KNt has little residence time in the ABC core central cavity.
source: By contrast, the KNt cryoEM density is absent in the apo structure, suggesting that when no ATP is bound to Kir6.2, KNt has little residence time in the ABC core central cavity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural observation.

claim: Despite not seeing KNt, the Kir6.2 channel is still closed in the dominant class structure of the apo state, likely due to loss of endogenous PIP2 during purification.
source: The fact that despite not seeing KNt, the Kir6.2 channel is still closed in the dominant class structure is likely due to loss of endogenous PIP2 during purification.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural observation.

claim: CBZ and RPG share the same binding pocket as GBC in KATP channels.
source: Our structures show that CBZ and RPG share the same binding pocket as GBC in KATP channels.
evidence: This is a primary structural finding of the study.

claim: There are no known structures of RPG and CBZ bound to proteins prior to this study.
source: Although both RPG and CBZ have been characterized extensively, with RPG being a commonly used oral hypoglycemic medication and CBZ an anticonvulsant, there are no known structures of these drugs bound to proteins.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the structural findings.

claim: The structures provide the first examples of how RPG and CBZ interact with their target proteins.
source: Thus, our structures provide the first examples of how these drugs interact with their target proteins.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the structural findings.

claim: Despite occupying a common pocket, each of the three compounds appear to form distinct chemical interactions with residues lining the binding pocket.
source: Despite occupying a common pocket, each of the three compounds appear to form distinct chemical interactions with residues lining the binding pocket.
evidence: This is a structural observation from comparing the three structures.

claim: CBZ is a well-known Nav channel blocker.
source: CBZ is a well-known Nav channel blocker (Lipkind and Fozzard, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: All ABC transporters share some structural similarities, in particular the ABC core structure.
source: Despite functional divergence, all ABC transporters share some structural similarities, in particular the ABC core structure (Thomas and Tampé, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ABC transporters, supported by citation.

claim: The Kir6.2 N-terminus can act as a plug or handle to regulate channel gating and assembly by inserting itself into the SUR1 ABC core central cavity formed by the two TM bundles.
source: An exciting finding here is how the Kir6.2 N-terminus can act as a plug or handle to regulate channel gating and assembly by inserting itself into the SUR1 ABC core central cavity formed by the two TM bundles.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion from the study.

claim: The exploitation of this structural space is akin to the mechanism by which viral peptide ICP47 enables immune-evasion of the pathogens.
source: The exploitation of this structural space is akin to the mechanism by which viral peptide ICP47 enables immune-evasion of the pathogens (Blees et al., 2017; Oldham et al., 2016; Parcej and Tampé, 2010).
evidence: This is a comparison to another system, supported by citations.

claim: Molecules which can reside within this space may offer opportunities for functional modulation of ABC transporters such as KATP.
source: Following this, molecules which can reside within this space may offer opportunities for functional modulation of ABC transporters such as KATP.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications.

claim: Application of a synthetic Kir6.2 N-terminal peptide (a.a. 2–33) to the cytoplasmic face of KATP channels in isolated membrane patches has been shown to increase KATP channel open probability.
source: Indeed, application of a synthetic Kir6.2 N-terminal peptide (a.a. 2–33) to the cytoplasmic face of KATP channels in isolated membrane patches has been shown to increase KATP channel open probability (Babenko and Bryan, 2002).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies, supported by citation.

claim: The exogenous peptide presumably competes with the N-terminus of Kir6.2 for binding to the SUR1 ABC core.
source: This is presumably due to competition of the exogenous peptide with the N-terminus of Kir6.2 for binding to the SUR1 ABC core.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional result.

claim: Both GBC and CBZ have been reported to bind or are substrates of other ABC transporters.
source: With regard to the drug binding pocket, it is worth noting that both GBC and CBZ have been reported to bind or are substrates of other ABC transporters (Zhou et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: The multidrug resistance transporter P-glycoprotein (ABCB1) recognizes several SUR1 ligands including GBC, albeit with much lower affinity.
source: For example, Bessadok et al. (2011) recently showed that the multidrug resistance transporter P-glycoprotein (ABCB1) recognizes several SUR1 ligands including GBC, albeit with much lower affinity.
evidence: This is based on another study, supported by citation.

claim: CBZ has been shown to correct the trafficking defect of ΔF508 CFTR (ABCC9), the most prevalent mutation underlying cystic fibrosis.
source: Moreover, CBZ has been shown to correct the trafficking defect of ΔF508 CFTR (ABCC9), the most prevalent mutation underlying cystic fibrosis (Carlile et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on another study, supported by citation.

claim: Other ABC transporters may recognize SUR1 ligands through a similar binding pocket identified here via conserved residues within the SUR1 GBC binding pocket such as R1246 and W1297.
source: An intriguing possibility is that these other ABC transporters recognize SUR1 ligands through a similar binding pocket identified here via conserved residues within the SUR1 GBC binding pocket such as R1246 and W1297.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential similarities across ABC transporters.
